sentences.text: America's debt trap can cost you a raise.
Your employer can make every payment and still cancel your promotion.
The trouble starts before anyone goes broke.
Imagine you own a workshop, and the machine loan comes due.
Your crew has orders waiting, but the bank sends a more expensive renewal quote.
The extra interest takes the money you set aside for another worker.
You delay the hire.
Your crew covers the extra orders.
The bank gets paid, and your business loses room to grow.
Stay for three checks you can run against public data to help protect your money from market mechanics.
Your own bills will show you where to start.
Working in Business Risk at JPMorgan taught me to look beyond whether someone made the payment.
I want to know what they gave up to make it.
Refinancing replaces an old loan with a new one, at a new price.
That renewal letter changes what the whole business can afford.
Follow that decision, because the owner who cuts back leaves an opening for somebody else.
A worker loses overtime, a customer pays more, and a competitor gains ground.
The need to refinance reaches beyond Washington.
Governments, businesses and households have old debt coming due, and they all need someone willing to finance the replacement.
The owner plans to put the next purchase on hold until borrowing gets cheaper, then pick up where the business left off.
Like the workshop, Washington has old debt coming due that must be refinanced at current borrowing costs.
Federal debt crossed forty trillion dollars in August.
Washington borrows to cover the gap between spending and revenue.
Through August, estimated net interest exceeded a trillion dollars for the fiscal year.
That was about twenty-two cents for every dollar of federal revenue.
Interest itself adds to the budget Washington has to finance.
Faster spending without matching revenue means more borrowing and more interest for future budgets.
That puts Washington in the market for money alongside businesses like our workshop.
On September seventeenth, twenty-year Treasury yields were above five percent.
Put yourself in the lender's seat.
You can earn that yield lending to Washington.
Why accept less from a business that might not pay you back?
The business has to compete with that alternative and pay for its own risks.
The Fed sets an overnight target; investors set the price of lending for years.
They weigh inflation, future policy and the risk of waiting to get their money back.
A Fed cut doesn't force those investors to accept less.
The renewal letter still has to offer a price a lender will accept.
But the existing loan comes due now.
The debt trap is having to accept the new borrowing cost because you can't afford to wait.
So the owner raises repair prices to cover the bigger interest bill.
Imagine a delivery company gets that bill for its vans.
The manager has a choice:
buy a replacement van or keep the old one working.
With repairs taking more of the budget, the manager postpones the purchase.
The vehicle dealer loses the sale.
If fewer orders mean less overtime, an employee takes home less pay.
And this squeeze isn't just for businesses; it reaches that employee's own bills.
Suppose that employee carries roughly sixty-six hundred dollars on a credit card charging twenty-two point four percent.
The annual interest is roughly fifteen hundred dollars if the balance stays put.
Losing overtime makes that existing bill harder to carry, even if the card's rate doesn't change.
Your first check is what the debt costs in dollars.
Multiply the balance by the annual rate for a rough interest bill, then compare it with the income paying it.
Use the actual statement for payments and compounding.
That comparison also helps explain why two businesses can face the same rates and head in opposite directions.
This is why I watch decisions that never become transactions.
A canceled hire doesn't appear in the default rate.
A postponed machine doesn't show up as a bankrupt factory.
Back at the workshop, the owner cancels a second machine planned for the expansion.
The equipment supplier had set aside production time for that order.
Now it needs another buyer.
Imagine a competitor offers a multiyear purchase agreement in exchange for a better price and a guaranteed delivery slot.
The supplier gets dependable orders.
The competitor gets the machine and room to negotiate.
The workshop's canceled order is another company's opening.
When demand returns, that competitor has the capacity to take it.
The workshop owner still has the old machine and a crew working around its limits.
That contest over the next machine is how I look at AI infrastructure.
Who can keep building while a rival has to stop?
The same funding squeeze that costs someone a raise can change who owns the equipment their employer needs.
Data centers need power, cooling and connections before they can serve customers.
A chip can't do much sitting in a building that hasn't been connected to the grid.
A builder can burn cash getting that capacity ready and still be worth backing.
I call that strategy accretive burn:
fund the build long enough to earn a valuable position.
The earnings don't have to outrun spending immediately.
The funding has to last until management can deliver.
A company borrowing because customers are leaving faces a different problem.
Your second check is who can finance the wait.
Your loan agreement tells you when a rate resets or a balance comes due.
For a public company, open its latest quarterly or annual report on the SEC's website.
Search for liquidity and debt maturities.
Add the company's construction-spending guidance and contractual commitments.
Compare the money it can use with the bills arriving before the project earns anything.
An undrawn credit line counts only if the company meets the conditions to use it.
Imagine a builder needs a hundred million dollars to finish and has sixty million available.
That leaves forty million to find before the project can earn its keep.
My tripwire is that forty-million-dollar gap.
Until committed funding closes it to zero, the project isn't fully funded.
A rival with the money secured can keep the crews working; this builder has to negotiate for another cheque.
Now put a real company's report beside that example.
NVIDIA's July balance sheet showed about twenty-two billion dollars in cash and equivalents, against one billion in short-term debt.
Those are two lines you can find yourself in the report linked below.
Other bills and commitments still count, so check those before treating the difference as spending money.
Then open the cash-flow table:
NVIDIA generated about twenty-one billion dollars in free cash flow during that quarter.
Its business was producing cash after capital spending, instead of needing investors to fund every next step.
That's why I watch a company like NVIDIA as a potential buyer of capacity when somebody else needs financing.
Remember the workshop owner who couldn't afford the next machine?
Now put NVIDIA on the other side of that negotiation.
Suppose NVIDIA's shares fall by a quarter, while a smaller infrastructure company's fall by two-thirds.
Both stocks fell.
But who has to sell, and who can afford to buy?
The smaller company still needs money to finish its site.
NVIDIA's cash flow gives it options:
fund the project, negotiate access, or pursue an acquisition.
A power connection doesn't become useless because its owner's shares fall.
What changes is who can afford to control it.
Your third check is what the runway buys.
Write management's promised delivery date beside your funding calculation.
In the next report, check whether customers could actually use what it built.
A finished shell without power won't do the job.
For NVIDIA, the same July report recorded eighty-nine billion dollars in data-center revenue, more than double the year before.
Customers were already paying for what the company supplied.
A new site still waiting for power hasn't reached that stage.
If a funded builder repeatedly misses delivery and needs more money to finish, my growth thesis was wrong.
These rising costs reach you through the decisions made around you.
An employer gives up a hire.
A customer cancels an order.
A supplier accepts a different buyer's terms.
The three checks fit together now.
What does the debt cost in dollars?
Who can finance the wait?
What is that time buying?
Use your statements for the household numbers and the public filings linked below for the businesses.
The renewal letter changed which workshop could afford to grow.
Your missing raise and the competitor's new machine came out of the same squeeze.
A business that keeps paying can still lose its future customers to a competitor that keeps building.
I want to know who will have to stop building and who can afford to buy what comes next.
